segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: I've been reading your personal statement, Paul. First, let's talk about your work experience in South America. What took you there? Was it to gain more fluency in Spanish?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Well, as I'm combining Spanish with Latin American studies, my main idea was to find out more about the way people lived there. My spoken 021 Spanish was already pretty good in fact.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: So you weren't too worried about language barriers?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: No. In fact, I ended up teaching English there, although that wasn't my original choice of work.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: I see. How did you find out about all this?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: I found an agency that runs all kinds of voluntary projects in South America.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: What kind of work?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Well, there were several possibilities.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: You mean construction? Engineeringwork?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Yes, getting involved in building projects was an option. Then there was tourism - taking tourists for walks around the volcanoes - which I actually 022 chose to do, and then there was work with local farmers.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: But you didn't continue with that project. Why not?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Because I never really knew whether I'd be needed or not. I'd thought it might be difficult physically, but I was certainly fit enough ... no, I wanted 023 to do something that had more of a proper structure to it, I suppose. I get de-motivatedotherwise.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: What do you think you learned from your experience? It must have been a great opportunityto examine community life.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Yes, but it was difficult at first to be accepted by the locals. It was a very remote village and some of them were reluctant to speak to me - although they were always interested in my clothes and how much I'd had to pay for them.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Well, that's understandable.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Yes, but things soon improved.What struck me was that when people 024 became more comfortablewith me and less suspicious, we really connectedwith each other in a meaningfulway.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: You made good 'friends?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Yes, with two of the families in particular.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Good. What about management.Did you have a project manager?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Yes and he gave me lots of advice and guidance. 025

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: And was he good at managingtoo?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: That wasn't his strong point! I think he was often more interested in the academicside of things than filing reports. He was a bit of a dreamer.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: And did you have a contract?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: I had to stay for a minimumof three months. My parentswere surprised when I asked to stay longer - six months in the e_nd.I was so happy there.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: And did anything on the administrationside of things surprise you? What was the food and lodging like?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Simple ... but there was plenty to eat and I only paid seven dollars a day for that which was amazing really. And they gave me all the equipment I needed ... even a laptop.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: You didn't expect that then?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: No.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Well, I'll look forward to hearing more.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: But now let's look at these modules.You'll need to start thinking about which ones you'll definitelywant to study. The first one here is Gender Studies in Latin America.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Mmm ...

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: It looks at how gender analysisis reconfiguringcivil society in Latin America. Women are increasinglyoccupyingpositions in governmentand in other elected leadershippositionsin Latin America. I think you'd find it interesting.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: If it was to do with people in the villages rather than those in the public sphere, I would.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Okay. What about Second LanguageAcquisition?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Do you think I'd find that useful?

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Well, you've had some practicalexperiencein the field, I think it would be.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: I hadn't thought about that. I'll put that down as a definite, then.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Okay. What about IndigenousWomen's Lives. That sounds appropriate.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: I thought so too, but I looked at last year's exam questions and that changed my mind.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Don't judge the value of the course on that. Maybe, talk to some other students first and we can talk about it again later.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Okay.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Yes. And lastly, will you sign up for Portugueselessons?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: My Spanish is good, so would I find that module easy?

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Not necessarily.Some peoplefind that Spanish interfereswith learning Portuguese... getting the accent right too. It's quite different in a lot of ways.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Well, I'd much sooner do somethingelse, then.

segments.speaker: WOMAN
segments.en: Alright. Now, what we need to do is ...
